Now let me compile everything into a verse-by-verse commentary. I'll draw from what I've gathered and note where gaps remain.

---

# Daniel 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Daniel 4 is unique in Scripture: it is a first-person testimony of a pagan king, Nebuchadnezzar, recounting his pride, humbling, madness, and restoration — and his acknowledgment of the sovereignty of the Most High God. Conservative commentators generally agree that Daniel incorporated this royal decree into his book under divine inspiration. The chapter is written in Aramaic (the language of Daniel 2:4–7:28).

- **Precept Austin** notes: the first three verses (vv. 1–3 in English Bibles) are numbered 3:31–33 in the Aramaic text; vv. 4–37 correspond to 4:1–34 in the Aramaic. Most authorities agree the content fits best with chapter 4. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)
- John MacArthur dates the events roughly between the 30th and 35th years of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, about 25–30 years after the fiery furnace incident (Daniel 3), when Daniel was about 45–50 years old. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)
- **Sam Storms** (charismatic/Reformed-leaning) notes the literary structure: the king begins and ends with praise (vv. 1–3 and 34–37), while the main story divides into the dream's narration (vv. 4–18) and its interpretation and fulfillment (vv. 19–33). (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 1 — "King Nebuchadnezzar, To the people of every nation and language..."

- **Gill**: The edict begins without pompous, extravagant titles (as Eastern monarchs typically used), just "Nebuchadnezzar the king" — evidence he was humbled under the mighty hand of God. The proclamation addresses "all people, nations, and languages," not limited to his own subjects; the king desired all in the known world to hear what God had done. "Peace be multiplied unto you" is the common Eastern salutation (*shalom* / *salaam*). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: This unique chapter is the testimony of a Gentile king. Nebuchadnezzar becomes a "witness" — one who relates what he has seen and experienced. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Precept Austin**: This is Nebuchadnezzar's "tract" — his personal witness to the saving hand of the Most High God. The contrast with Daniel 3:4,7 is striking: the same phrase "peoples, nations and men of every language" was previously used to order idolatrous worship; now it announces the true God. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)

---

## v. 2 — "I am pleased to declare the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me."

- **Gill**: The phrase "I thought it good" literally means "fair" or "beautiful" — it was highly becoming, his duty, and profitable for others. The "signs and wonders" include the dream itself, its interpretation, its exact fulfillment, and his restoration. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: It is good to declare what God has done. Satan has a huge interest in keeping believers unnaturally silent about God's works. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics**: The recounting of Divine dealings should be marked by public concern and propriety. Nebuchadnezzar's facts were notorious; it rested with him to exhibit them in a divine light. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/daniel/4.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "How great are His signs... His kingdom is an eternal kingdom..."

- **Gill**: The signs are great beyond expression; no power of nature, earth, or hell can resist them. Nebuchadnezzar had learned from Daniel 2:44 that God's kingdom is everlasting, while his own reign — though long — would end. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik**: Nebuchadnezzar recognized God's kingdom was far greater than his own, and God's dominion was completely unique because it is everlasting. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: Even when in history it seems God is in retreat or evil runs unchecked, God's kingdom and rule continue undiminished from generation to generation. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 4 — "I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace."

- **Gill**: The king was at rest from all enemies, having returned from victorious wars, enjoying health, riches, sensual pleasures, and universal fame. Gill dates this around the 35th year of his reign. "Flourishing" or "green" (*ra'anan*) pictures a luxuriant tree — ironically apt for the dream to follow. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik**: This rest was the false peace of the ungodly; God would soon shake him from false security. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Precept Austin** (quoting J. Vernon McGee): The king begins with "perpendicular 'I'-itis" — the fatal malady of pride infecting all mankind. The chapter traces his journey from arrogant "I" to humble acknowledgment of the Most High God. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)
- **Sam Storms**: The picture is of the successful, satisfied potentate — not unlike the rich landowner in Luke 12:15–21. "What could possibly disturb this scene of tranquility and confidence?" (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 5 — "I had a dream, and it frightened me..."

- **Gill**: Though Nebuchadnezzar did not understand the dream, he perceived it portended some evil, throwing him into a panic. God can make the minds of the greatest men uneasy amidst all their glory, pride, and pleasure. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)

---

## vv. 6–7 — The wise men summoned; they cannot interpret.

- **Gill**: Unlike Daniel 2, the king could remember and tell the dream. The wise men had previously promised that if the dream were told, they could interpret it — but now they could not, exposing their fraud. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik**: The dream was fairly easy to interpret; the wise men probably lacked courage more than insight. Nebuchadnezzar said "they did not make known," not that they *could* not. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: The text is ambiguous — it may not be that they were *unable* but *unwilling*, for reasons similar to those that made Daniel himself hesitate (v. 19). However, see v. 18 where the king says they were "not able." (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 8 — "But at last, into my presence came Daniel..."

- **Guzik** (quoting Trapp): "And why 'at last'? Why was he not sooner sent for? If the soothsayers and sorcerers could have served the turn, Daniel had never been sought to. This is the guise of graceless men; they run not to God till all other refuges fail them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Gill**: Daniel's late arrival was ordered by Providence so the magicians' incompetence would first be exposed, and God would be glorified. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Sam Storms** offers multiple explanations: (1) Nebuchadnezzar had forgotten Daniel after many years; (2) Nebuchadnezzar remembered all too well and, knowing the dream likely foretold his humiliation at the hands of Daniel's God, wanted nothing to do with either (Calvin's view); (3) custom demanded the chief be summoned last; (4) Daniel was considered more an officer of state than a wise man; (5) Daniel intentionally waited until the ignorance of the court magicians was manifest so that God's power would be all the more glorious. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)
- **Guzik** on "whose name is Belteshazzar after the name of my god": Before this chapter, the king still considered the Babylonian deity Bel his god. Being impressed with God isn't the same as being converted. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## v. 9 — "O Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you..."

- **Gill**: Nebuchadnezzar speaks in his heathenish manner — either referring to many gods (some holy, some impure), or, influenced by Jewish speech, meaning the one true God who alone gives the spirit of prophecy. "No secret troubleth thee" — nothing perplexes your mind; all is plain before you. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)

---

## vv. 10–12 — The great tree in the dream.

- **Gill**: The tree is an emblem of a powerful prince — well settled, strongly supported. Babylon was in the midst of the then-known world. The tree's height reaching heaven expresses Nebuchadnezzar's dominion over all nations — or his ambition of deity itself (cf. Isaiah 14:14). Its visibility "to the end of all the earth" reflects his worldwide fame. The branches represent provinces or governors; the abundant fruit, great revenues; the beasts under it, the more barbarous nations; the birds in its branches, the more civilized (including Israel). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik**: The tree was noted for size, strength, prominence, beauty, fruit, and shelter — all of which would be lost. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## v. 13 — "a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven."

- **Gill**: "Watcher" — so called because angels are incorporeal, ever watch, never sleep, and are always attentive to God's commands. In the fragment of Enoch, angels are called *egregori* (watchers). Some lexicons render the word "an enemy" based on 1 Samuel 28:16, suggesting angels can be hostile to the wicked. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Sam Storms**: Most likely an angelic being — one among many whom God has assigned to watch over human activities and in some sense mediate God's rule. The word "angelic" is not in the original text. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## vv. 14–15 — "Cut down the tree... But leave the stump with its roots... a band of iron and bronze..."

- **Gill**: "Hew down the tree" = remove the monarch from his throne. "Cut off his branches" = take away provinces. "Shake off his leaves" = cause deputy governors to abandon allegiance. "Scatter his fruit" = let others take the revenues. "Leave the stump" = let him not be utterly destroyed; his life is preserved, with hope of restoration (cf. Job 14:7 — a tree cut to the stump may revive). The "band of iron and brass" alludes to binding madmen with chains (cf. Mark 5:4). The "tender grass of the field" = instead of a palace, he will dwell in the field. "Wet with the dew of heaven" = he would lie all night exposed to the elements — the word has the sense of "being dipped" as in a dyer's vat. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik**: The band of iron and bronze was either for the stump's confinement or protection; the tree (man) would no longer be free and great. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: The stump indicates Nebuchadnezzar will survive to rule again. The band may symbolize his preservation, or as Young and Keil suggest, the fetter of insanity withdrawing his freedom. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 16 — "Let his mind be changed from that of a man, and let him be given the mind of a beast till seven times pass him by."

- **Gill**: His rational soul did not depart (he would have died), but the powers of his soul were vitiated and depraved: his understanding imagined himself a beast; his judgment could not distinguish beastly from human actions; his memory of past things failed; his will and fancy ran toward brutal things, deserts, fields, and grass, and he shunned human society. "Seven times" means seven years (as in Daniel 7:25) — the same length of time Solomon's temple was built, which Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)

---

## v. 17 — "This decision is the decree of the watchers... so that the living will know that the Most High rules..."

- **Gill**: Angels are not authors of the decree but approvers and ready executors of it — alluding to the manner of kings who consult their privy council (cf. 1 Kings 22:19), though properly speaking this is only after the manner of men. Some understand "holy ones" as saints on earth who requested God's judgments upon this proud monarch in prayer. Yet Gill favors interpreting the whole of the three Persons of the Godhead. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **John MacArthur (GTY)**: This verse contains the key phrase of the entire chapter: "that the living may know that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men." It is repeated in v. 25, v. 32, and echoed in v. 34. The whole chapter is set to teach that no man can set himself above God. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/27-12/how-are-the-mighty-fallen)
- **Guzik**: In light of this, the dream wasn't hard to interpret — it clearly dealt with the humbling of a great king. No wonder none of the counselors wanted to interpret it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Ellicott**: The decree and demand are from the angelic watchers — the heavenly council. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/4.htm)

---

## v. 18 — "Now, Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation..."

- **Guzik**: Nebuchadnezzar knew he could get an honest answer from Daniel, even when the truth was hard. Though he recognized Daniel as filled with the Spirit of the Holy God, Nebuchadnezzar had not yet yielded himself to that God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## v. 19 — "For a time, Daniel... was perplexed, and his thoughts alarmed him."

- **Guzik**: Daniel genuinely cared for Nebuchadnezzar and was troubled by the dream's meaning. He didn't want it to be true of his friend. His words "may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!" reflect his genuine love. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: Daniel's hesitation mirrors the reason the court magicians may have hesitated — they feared telling the king such hard truth. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## vv. 20–22 — "You, O king, are that tree!"

- **Guzik**: Daniel applied the point without ambiguity. Instead of reaching for a general point (e.g., "We all could use a little more humility"), he brought the truth in love. This parallels Nathan's words to David: "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Guzik** (quoting Clarke): "Great men and princes are often represented, in the language of the prophets, under the similitude of trees, see Ezekiel 17:5–6; 31:3 and following; Jeremiah 22:15; Psalm 1:3; 37:35." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## vv. 23–25 — The interpretation: the king will be driven away, eat grass like an ox, until he acknowledges God's rule.

- **Guzik**: When Daniel explained this, the king probably couldn't guess just how literally it would be fulfilled. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Ellicott**: On v. 25 — "They shall drive thee" is the third person plural active with an impersonal subject, frequently standing for the second person singular passive: "thou shalt be driven" (cf. Luke 16:9). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/4.htm)

---

## v. 26 — "As for the command to leave the stump of the tree with its roots, your kingdom will be restored to you..."

- **Guzik**: This was God's intended purpose — the king could have avoided the humiliating fate if he had genuinely humbled himself. "After you come to know that Heaven rules" was the goal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## v. 27 — "Break away from your sins by doing what is right... Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity."

- **Guzik**: The right reaction to the threat of judgment is humble repentance. Nebuchadnezzar should have followed the example of Nineveh at Jonah's preaching. He was counseled not only to stop sinning but to practice righteousness and generosity — specifically "showing mercy to the poor." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: Daniel called on the king to break off sins of idolatry and rebellion, and to show mercy to the poor (cf. Isaiah 55:7; 58:7; Ezekiel 18:7; 1 Peter 4:8). To turn to the Lord might lengthen his tranquility. Hezekiah turned and his days were lengthened; Nineveh repented and was spared. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-4.html)
- **Sam Storms** (quoting Young): Young differs from most: he argues the predicted madness was to come for the express purpose of converting Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel's exhortation was not to avert judgment but so that his period of prosperity *after restoration* might be lengthened. "The text says nothing of an averting of the predicted judgment, but merely speaks of a lengthening of a period of tranquility." (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 28 — "All this happened to King Nebuchadnezzar."

- **Guzik**: This verse transitions the narrative from the dream/interpretation to fulfillment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## vv. 29–30 — Twelve months later, the king's boast: "Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built..."

- **Guzik**: God gave Nebuchadnezzar twelve months to repent. He probably forgot about the dream during that time — but God did not. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Enduring Word** on the historicity: Daniel knew that the new Babylon was the creation of Nebuchadnezzar — something previously thought untrue and only verified by recent archaeology. In the British Museum, six columns of writing recovered from Babylon describe his huge building projects. Most excavated bricks carry his stamp. Late-daters of Daniel (who place it in the Maccabean period, c. 167 B.C.) cannot explain how a late writer would know to attribute Babylon's spectacular buildings to Nebuchadnezzar. Liberal commentator R. H. Pfeiffer said of this problem: "We shall presumably never know." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: Babylon was truly great. Its outer double wall was 17 miles long, wide enough for two chariots to race side by side. The Ishtar Gate, the processional street with enameled brick lions and dragons, over 50 temples, and the Hanging Gardens (one of the Seven Wonders) — built especially for his wife who missed the mountains of Media — all attested to his boast. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## vv. 31–32 — The voice from heaven: "It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar..."

- **Guzik**: The announcement came in the same words he heard in his dream. This showed him the dream was about to be fulfilled. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## v. 33 — The judgment fulfilled: he ate grass like an ox; his hair grew like eagles' feathers and his nails like birds' claws.

- **Enduring Word / Guzik**: The form of insanity in which a person thinks themselves an animal and imitates its behavior has been clinically observed. It is called generally *insania zoanthropica*, and specifically in Nebuchadnezzar's case, *boanthropy* — the delusion that one is an ox. Walvoord quotes Dr. Raymond Harrison of Britain, who in 1946 treated a patient suffering from boanthropy, identical to Nebuchadnezzar's condition. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: R. K. Harrison (Introduction to the Old Testament) describes this as a rare form of monomania. Harrison personally encountered a boanthropy patient in a British mental institution in 1946 — a man who ate only grass, drank only water, never wore a coat, yet was in superb physical condition with firm muscles, bright eyes, and apparent immunity to disease. His hair was lengthened and fingernails coarse and thickened — precisely the physical conditions of Daniel 4:33. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)
- **Ellicott**: This malady is now for the most part agreed to be a form of mania known as lycanthropy. It appears, however, from Daniel that he retained consciousness, as "he lifted up his eyes to heaven" (v. 34) before his "understanding" returned. Berosus, the Babylonian historian, records nothing of this except the vague statement that "Nebuchadnezzar fell sick and died after a reign of forty-three years." It is remarkable that an interval is mentioned in his inscriptions during which he executed no great public works. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik on historicity**: There is no corresponding record of this seven-year period in secular Babylonian records — exactly as expected, since Near Eastern leaders trumpeted achievements and hid embarrassments. However, there is no historical record of Nebuchadnezzar's governmental activity between 582 B.C. and 575 B.C. — a deafening silence. Abydenus, a Greek historian (268 B.C.), wrote that Nebuchadnezzar was "possessed by some god" and "immediately disappeared." Walvoord: "Although critics have imagined a series of incredible objections... the narrative actually reads very sensibly and the objections seem trivial and unsupported." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)

---

## vv. 34–35 — Nebuchadnezzar's restoration and praise.

- **Guzik**: Nebuchadnezzar could not break free until God appointed the end of the time. Then he had the opportunity to humble himself and lift his eyes to heaven. He could only see the truth about himself when he first saw the truth about God. The return of reason results in worship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Ellicott**: "Lifted up mine eyes" — a sign of seeking help from heaven (cf. Psalm 123:1). By "understanding" is meant not so much consciousness as his sense of personality, which had been lost for a time. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/4.htm)
- **Guzik** (quoting Spurgeon): "We do not worship enough, my brethren. Even in our public gatherings we do not have enough worship. O worship the King! Bow your heads now — bow your spirits rather, and adore him that liveth for ever and ever." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Sam Storms**: The affirmation of divine omnipotence in v. 35 emphasizes the insolence of disputing with God. The language about restraining His hand is taken from the custom of striking/spanking the hand of a child who reaches for something off-limits. How dare we treat God that way! "No one can slap his hand and question his right to act as he chooses." (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

---

## v. 36 — "My honor and splendor returned to me... and surpassing greatness was added to me."

- **Guzik**: God wanted to restore Nebuchadnezzar. The goal wasn't to bring him low, but to bring him to his proper place before God and among men. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: His majesty, like Job's, was greater than ever before — "For everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted" (Job 42:12; Proverbs 22:4; Luke 18:14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-4.html)
- **MacArthur (GTY)**: Even the counselors and lords sought him out — they didn't say, "Don't go near that raving maniac who's been freaked out for seven years." (https://www.gty.org/sermons/27-12/how-are-the-mighty-fallen)

---

## v. 37 — "Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven... He is able to humble those who walk in pride."

- **Guzik**: The abiding lesson: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). There have been many who rise from humble origins to great glory and then fall — most, if not all, through pride. A proud look is number one on God's list of most hated sins (Proverbs 6:16–19). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-4/)
- **MacArthur (GTY)**: This is the spiritual biography of Nebuchadnezzar — an incredible, astounding man, one of the geniuses of human history, puffed and proud as ruler of the world, and how God literally crushes him into nothing and turns him around through another dream. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/27-12/how-are-the-mighty-fallen)

---

## Major Point of Debate: Was Nebuchadnezzar Genuinely Converted?

This is the most significant disagreement among Protestant commentators on this chapter:

### Those who say YES (genuine conversion):

- **E. J. Young** (Reformed): (1) There is discernible progress in his knowledge of God (cf. 2:47 → 3:28 → 4:34–35). (2) He acknowledges God's utter sovereignty over his own experience. (3) He makes true statements about God's omnipotence. (4) He worships this God, identifying Him as "King of heaven." "Although the faith of Nebuchadnezzar may indeed have been weak and his knowledge meagre, yet his faith was saving faith, and his knowledge true." (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)
- **H. A. Ironside** (Brethren): The chapter "seems clearly to show that a work of grace took place in his soul." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)
- **Precept Austin**: Nebuchadnezzar's testimony explains "how the Most High God caused him to be born again." If so, this is the only chapter in Scripture written by a new believer. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: "It appears that Nebuchadnezzar was now saved, Romans 10:13." The commentary traces three steps in his recognition of God: (1) a God among gods (2:47); (2) a Hebrew deity who delivers (3:28); (3) a personal God whom he has offended and from whom he found forgiveness (4:34–35). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-4.html)
- **Sam Storms**: Adds to Young's arguments Nebuchadnezzar's statement of faith in God's "truth" and "justice" (4:37). "Although we can't be certain, I believe he was genuinely converted." (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)

### Those who say NO or are uncertain:

- **Joyce Baldwin** (evangelical Anglican): She contends his reference to God as "the King of heaven" (v. 37) is impersonal and keeps God at a distance — "appears to fall short of penitence and true faith." Also, if truly saved, why didn't he restore Israel's religious culture, release captives, or display fruits of regeneration? (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-4:1-37)
- **Gill** (older Baptist): "Whether his conversion was real is not evident" — though Gill acknowledges the king expresses himself in stronger language about God than ever before. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/4.htm)
- **Dr. Constable**: "It is difficult to prove conclusively from the text that the monarch placed saving faith in Yahweh, but that is a distinct possibility... Only God knows for sure." He notes that Leupold, Archer, and Baldwin all held he did not become a believer in a saving sense. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-4.html)
- **John MacArthur**: MacArthur calls it "conversion" (his Study Bible note says "he converted to such worship of the true God") but in the sermon he frames it more broadly: Nebuchadnezzar is a "symbol" of what God does with proud rulers, and also a warning to every individual. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/27-12/how-are-the-mighty-fallen)

---

## Other Views (limited by search availability)

I was unable to search specifically for Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com), or modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) perspectives due to search limits being reached. However, I can note:

- **Precept Austin** references the **Apologetics Study Bible**, which notes that critical scholars consider Daniel 4 to be literary fiction derived from the "Prayer of Nabonidus" (4QPrNab), an Aramaic fragment found at Qumran in 1952. However, differences (name of king, nature of illness, location) far outweigh similarities, and the Nabonidus story is "doubtless a distorted version or later application of the biblical narrative." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)

- **Precept Austin** also notes that liberal scholars rejected Daniel 4 as authentic for several reasons, but the Qumran text of Daniel (which on critics' own criteria requires Daniel to be much older than the 2nd century B.C.) now challenges that conclusion. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_4_commentary)

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Common Agreement |
|---|---|
| God's sovereignty over rulers | All traditions affirm this as the central message (v. 17, 25, 32, 34–35) |
| Pride brings judgment | Universally affirmed; James 4:6 / Proverbs 16:18 |
| The historicity of the account | Conservative traditions affirm; liberal/critical traditions question, attributing to the "Prayer of Nabonidus" |
| Nebuchadnezzar's salvation | **Major disagreement**: some say yes (Ironside, Young, Storms, Precept Austin, Garner-Howes), some say no/uncertain (Baldwin, Archer, Leupold, Gill) |
| "Seven times" = seven years | Near-universal agreement among traditional commentators |
| Boanthropy as clinical condition | Widely cited by evangelicals as confirming historicity |
| The chapter as personal testimony | Universally noted as unique in Scripture — a Gentile king's own witness |
